title: Shakuhachi
summary: The shakuhachi is a Japanese flute cut from the thick root end of a bamboo stem. It is blown across a sharp notch at the open top, with four finger holes on the front and one more hole behind. Players bend each note with breath and head angle, so a few notes can sound like a whole landscape.
howToPlay: Six lanes stand for the notes of the flute's five-note family, from the lowest, Ro, to the same note an octave higher.
Beside each lane the flute shows its five holes: glowing ones are covered, dark ones are open, and the dashed ring is the hole behind, closed by the thumb.
Notes travel down the tube toward a hole; strike the lane just as a note arrives and let the long ones ring.
Bend the note like a real player: while a note rings, drag down to flatten it (meri) or up to sharpen it (kari). The bend is for expression and is never scored.
Start with the five steps up the mountain, then try the one long breath and the echo between the ridges.
rules: The flute has five notes in a pentatonic family: Ro, Tsu, Re, Chi and Ri, plus Ro again an octave up.
Covering all holes gives the lowest note; each higher note lifts fingers in the flute's real pattern, including the thumb hole behind.
A stroke within a hair of the note is perfect, a near one is good, and a missed one scores nothing.
An extra stroke while a song is running costs a few points.
Three stars need roughly nine notes in ten on time.
heritageNote: The shakuhachi has been played in Japan for many centuries, as a flute for solo pieces and later in chamber ensembles. Makers still cut each flute from a single bamboo root, and the fingerings shown follow the common five-hole pattern.
credits: Tradition: shakuhachi playing; melodies written for this game
